name: Parji
confidence_why: No description of Parji word stress exists: the only grammar, Burrow & Bhattacharya (1953), says nothing about stress or accent, and the expectation of non-phonemic word-initial stress rests solely on family-wide generalisations about Dravidian in Zvelebil (1970), Sjoberg (1971) and Krishnamurti (2003), none of which examined Parji.
catalog_citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages (Cambridge Language Surveys). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (family-level statement of record, sec. 1.5.1, p. 27). The only Parji grammar, Burrow, T. & S. Bhattacharya. 1953. The Parji Language: A Dravidian Language of Bastar. Hertford: Stephen Austin & Sons, is does not discuss stress.
catalog_locator: Krishnamurti 2003 sec. 1.5.1 'Phonology' (within 1.5 Typological features of the Dravidian languages), p. 27; consulted again from the on-disk CUP/ProQuest chapter-1 PDF, p. 30, running head '1.5 Typological features of Dravidian 27' (extract). Parji identity: p. 26 entry '21. Parji (Poroja, Dhurwa)'. Sec. 2.4.1 'Stress and intonation', p. 59, known only from Google Books; it treats Tamil and Telugu only. Burrow & Bhattacharya 1953 ch. I 'Orthography and Phonology' pp. 1-8: both archive.org OCRs in the copy consulted re-a full-text search for stress/accent, 0 hits for stress/accent/prominence/intonation/pitch (the only 'loud' matches are 'cloud' and scan noise).
catalog_quote: The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each). The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for duru1236. This work gives a family-wide generalisation (initial, non-phonemic) that covers Parji only by scope; the only language-specific stress statements in the book's sec. 2.4.1 are about Tamil and Telugu. Parji appears at p. 26 only as list entry '21. Parji (Poroja, Dhurwa)' with Burrow & Bhattacharya (1953) as the source. The listed archive.org open copy is an ERIC microfiche abstract card (ED 475 049, one page, 'Document Not Available From EDRS'), not the book; the p. 27 text was read from the on-disk ProQuest chapter-1 file and sec. 2.4.1 from Google Books feed snippets.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement: no Dravidian language has phonemic stress; stress (loudness) normally falls on the initial syllable of the word regardless of its length, and a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Sec. 2.4.1 gives language-specific detail only for Tamil (non-contrastive, first syllable) and Telugu (experimental: first syllable if short, otherwise the second syllable when it follows a short syllable and has a long vowel). Nothing is said about Parji.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec. 2.4.1 mentions 'secondary stress' in a Tamil example list (kudira 'horse', pattālakkāran 'soldier'); the snippet does not show the rule and it is Tamil, not Parji.
new_statements.exceptions: Telugu (sec. 2.4.1, after Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991) is weight-sensitive: stress on the second syllable when it has a long vowel after a short first syllable. p. 27 notes a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. None of this is stated for Parji.
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti 2003 p. 26 lists the language as '21. Parji (Poroja, Dhurwa). Pop. 44,001 in the Bastar district of Madhya Pradesh and the adjacent hills of the Koraput district of Orissa. Burrow and Bhattacharya (1953).' under III. Central Dravidian; no dialect is singled out. Zvelebil 1970 names Parji only in language lists and the bibliography. No work opened here describes a particular Parji/Duruwa dialect.

new_statements.quote: 1.10.10. There is so far no clear evidence for dynamic accent having distinctive phonemic value in any Dr. language. In other words, accent ("stress") seems to be predictable (the primary stress always on the first, i.e. radical, syllable) and therefore non-distinctive. This does not mean, however, that, phonetically speaking, dynamic stress is absent in Dr. languages; it is of course present on the subphonemic level, and also, so to say, metalinguistically. The same is true about pitch. [...] while there is probably not a (dynamic) stress contrast in any Dr. language present, we cannot speak at all about intonationless speech when discussing Dravidian
